questions.question: How do you set up a Mockito test class in JUnit 5?
questions.title: Mockito Test Setup JUnit 5 | Java Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: **Add `@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)` to the class, declare `@Mock` for dependencies, and `@InjectMocks` for the class under test.** MockitoExtension processes these annotations automatically before each test, no manual setup needed.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical Mockito setup — can you write a test class from scratch?
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Forgetting @ExtendWith and wondering why @Mock is null
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show a complete test class skeleton with all annotations in context

sections.title: Complete Test Class Structure
Key Points
sections.content:
- @ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class): activates Mockito annotations
- @Mock: creates a mock for each annotated field
- @InjectMocks: creates the class under test and injects @Mock fields
- Mocks are reset before each test automatically
- Alternative: MockitoAnnotations.openMocks(this) in @BeforeEach
- Strictness: MockitoExtension uses STRICT_STUBS by default (unused stubs = error)
- Verify no unexpected interactions: verifyNoMoreInteractions()

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: I annotate the test class with @ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class). Then I declare each dependency as a @Mock field — Mockito creates fake instances. I annotate the class being tested with @InjectMocks — Mockito creates a real instance and injects the mocks. Before each test, all mocks are reset automatically. In a test method I stub mock behavior with when-thenReturn in the Arrange phase, call the method in the Act phase, and verify the result and any expected interactions in the Assert phase. The MockitoExtension also uses strict stubbing mode by default, which fails the test if I declare a stub that's never called — helps keep tests clean.

questions.question: What is strict stubbing mode in Mockito and why is it useful?
questions.title: Mockito Strict Stubbing | Java Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: **Strict stubbing fails tests if a stub is declared but never called, or called with different arguments.** It prevents test pollution from outdated or incorrect stubs. MockitoExtension enables STRICT_STUBS by default in Mockito 2.23+.

interviewer_intent.testing: Depth of Mockito knowledge — shows you've used it seriously
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Getting errors from STRICT_STUBS and disabling it instead of fixing the unnecessary stub
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that STRICT_STUBS improves test quality by catching stale stubs that indicate test drift

sections.title: Clean Up After Yourself
sections.content: STRICT_STUBS reports two types of problems: (1) **Unnecessary stubbing**: `when(mock.method()).thenReturn(x)` declared but never invoked during the test. (2) **Stubbing argument mismatch**: stub set up with certain args but called with different args. Without STRICT_STUBS these are silent — tests pass with stale stubs. With STRICT_STUBS, these become test failures forcing developers to keep stubs accurate.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- STRICT_STUBS: default with MockitoExtension
- Fails on: unused stubs, stubbing argument mismatches
- Prevents test pollution from outdated setup
- Disable per test: @MockitoSettings(strictness = LENIENT)
- Disable per stub: lenient().when(mock.method()).thenReturn(x)
- STRICT_STUBS catches: copy-paste errors, outdated setup
- Improves test signal quality — every stub is actively used

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: Strict stubbing mode, which is the default with MockitoExtension in modern Mockito, fails the test if I declare a stub that's never called during the test. This is useful because it prevents test pollution — if I copy a test and forget to remove a stub that's no longer relevant, strict stubbing immediately tells me. It also catches argument mismatches where I stub one argument but the code calls with a different argument. Without strict mode, these would silently pass even though my stubs weren't doing anything useful. If I genuinely need a lenient stub, I can annotate it specifically with lenient().when().

questions.question: How do you create a mock manually without annotations in Mockito?
questions.title: Mockito.mock() Manual Creation | Java Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: **Use `Mockito.mock(ClassName.class)` to create a mock programmatically.** This is equivalent to `@Mock` but done inline. Use it when you need to create a mock dynamically or outside a test class context — e.g., in a helper method or when the class is generic.

interviewer_intent.testing: Knowledge of both annotation and programmatic Mockito styles
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing the manual form — only knowing @Mock annotation
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain when you'd choose manual creation over annotations: dynamic mocking, generic types, factory methods

sections.title: Programmatic Mock Creation
sections.content: `OrderRepository mockRepo = Mockito.mock(OrderRepository.class)`. Equivalent to `@Mock`. After creation, use normally: `when(mockRepo.findById(1L)).thenReturn(Optional.of(order))`. For generic types: `@SuppressWarnings("unchecked") List<String> mockList = Mockito.mock(List.class)` or use `@Mock List<String> mockList` (annotation handles generics more cleanly). `Mockito.spy(new ArrayList<>())` is the equivalent for spies.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Mockito.mock(Class.class): creates a mock without @Mock
- Mockito.spy(new RealObject()): creates a spy without @Spy
- Used in: helper methods, static contexts, dynamic mock creation
- Same capabilities as @Mock — all stubbing/verify works the same
- Generic mocks: annotations handle type erasure better
- Mockito.mockStatic(Class.class): mock static methods (Mockito 3.4+)
- Mockito.reset(mock): reset a mock's stubbing and interactions

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: Besides @Mock annotations, I can create mocks programmatically with Mockito.mock passing the class. The result behaves identically — I can stub it with when-thenReturn and verify calls on it. I'd use the programmatic form when I need to create a mock in a helper method, a factory method for test data, or dynamically based on a condition. The annotation form is cleaner for the standard case of declaring dependencies in a test class. For spies, the equivalent is Mockito.spy wrapping a real instance. Mockito also has mockStatic for mocking static methods, which requires a try-with-resources block to scope the mock.

questions.question: How do you verify that a method was never called in Mockito?
questions.title: Mockito verify never() | Java Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: **Use `verify(mock, never()).method(args)` to assert a method was NOT called.** Also useful: `verifyNoInteractions(mock)` — asserts no methods were called on the mock. Use these to test negative scenarios like 'email should not be sent when order fails validation'.

interviewer_intent.testing: Negative testing with Mockito — important for verifying side effects don't happen
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing how to verify a method wasn't called — only knowing verify() for positive cases
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give a concrete scenario: when validation fails, the database save should NOT be called

sections.title: Verifying Absence of Calls
sections.content: `verify(emailService, never()).sendEmail(any())` — fails if sendEmail was called. `verifyNoInteractions(emailService)` — fails if ANY method was called on emailService. `verifyNoMoreInteractions(emailService)` — fails if any method was called that wasn't already verified. Use never() for specific methods, verifyNoInteractions for the whole mock.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- verify(mock, never()).method(args): specific method not called
- verifyNoInteractions(mock): no methods called on this mock
- verifyNoMoreInteractions(mock): no unverified interactions
- times(n): verify called exactly n times
- atLeast(n), atMost(n), atLeastOnce(): flexible counts
- Use case: validation fail → no DB save, no email sent
- Important: test both the happy path AND the negative path

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: To verify a method was NOT called, I use verify with the never() modifier — verify emailService comma never, dot sendEmail. If the method was called, the test fails. For asserting that absolutely no methods were called on a mock, I use verifyNoInteractions passing the mock object. For example, when testing that validation failure prevents any database writes, I'd verify the repository's save method was never called after the validation error. This kind of negative verification is just as important as positive verification — it confirms side effects don't happen when they shouldn't.

questions.question: How do you set up Mockito in a Spring Boot project?
questions.title: Mockito Setup in Spring Boot
questions.direct_answer: Spring Boot's spring-boot-starter-test dependency includes Mockito automatically; add @ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class) for pure unit tests.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know how Mockito fits into the Spring Boot test ecosystem without manual configuration
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Manually adding mockito-core when spring-boot-starter-test already provides it, causing version conflicts
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Distinguish between mockito-core, mockito-junit-jupiter, and when each is needed

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
In a Spring Boot project you typically do not need to add Mockito manually because spring-boot-starter-test, which is included in every Spring Boot project by default in the test scope, already pulls in mockito-core and mockito-junit-jupiter for you. So step one is just making sure you have that starter in your pom.xml or build.gradle.

For pure unit tests — tests that do not load a Spring context — you annotate your test class with @ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class). This enables @Mock, @Spy, @Captor, and @InjectMocks annotations and also activates strict stubbing, which catches unused stubs and makes tests more reliable.

For integration tests that do load a Spring context you would use @SpringBootTest instead, and in that case you would use @MockBean rather than @Mock to replace a real Spring bean with a Mockito mock inside the application context.

If you ever need a specific Mockito version that differs from what Spring Boot manages, you can override it in the properties section of your pom.xml with the mockito.version property, but that is rarely necessary.

sections.title: Key Points
content: spring-boot-starter-test includes Mockito — no separate dependency needed
@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class) activates Mockito annotations for pure unit tests
@SpringBootTest + @MockBean is the pattern for integration tests
Override mockito.version in pom.xml properties to pin a specific version

questions.question: What is the difference between Mockito.mock() and the @Mock annotation?
questions.title: Mockito.mock() vs @Mock Annotation
questions.direct_answer: Mockito.mock(Class.class) creates mocks programmatically, while @Mock is annotation-based and requires MockitoExtension or MockitoAnnotations.openMocks() to initialize.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand both styles and can explain why the annotation approach is preferred in modern tests
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using @Mock without @ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class) and then wondering why mocks are null
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that @ExtendWith also enables strict stubbing which catches bugs that the programmatic approach misses by default

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
Mockito.mock(SomeClass.class) is the programmatic way to create a mock — you call it explicitly, usually in a @BeforeEach setup method or directly in the test, and you assign the result to a field or variable. This approach is self-contained but verbose, especially when you have multiple dependencies.

The @Mock annotation is the declarative, cleaner alternative. You annotate a field in your test class with @Mock and Mockito creates and injects the mock for you. However, @Mock does nothing on its own — you need to activate it. There are two ways: annotate the test class with @ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class), which is the modern JUnit 5 approach and is recommended; or call MockitoAnnotations.openMocks(this) in a @BeforeEach method, which is the older style.

The @ExtendWith approach is preferred because it also enables strict stubbing mode, which will fail your test if you set up a stub that is never actually called — this catches copy-paste errors and dead code in your tests. Both approaches produce functionally equivalent mocks, but @Mock with MockitoExtension is cleaner, less repetitive, and gives you better feedback on test quality.

sections.title: Key Points
content: Mockito.mock() is programmatic; @Mock is annotation-based and more concise
@ExtendWith is preferred — it enables strict stubbing which catches unused stubs

questions.question: What does MockitoSession do and how does it differ from MockitoJUnitRunner?
questions.title: MockitoSession vs MockitoJUnitRunner
questions.direct_answer: MockitoSession is a programmatic, JUnit-agnostic way to initialise mocks and enforce strict stubbing; MockitoJUnitRunner is a JUnit 4-specific runner that does the same automatically.

interviewer_intent.testing: Familiarity with different Mockito initialisation approaches and their trade-offs
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using MockitoJUnitRunner in a JUnit 5 project where it is not supported
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that MockitoSession is preferred in JUnit 5 or framework-agnostic contexts and enforces strictness without requiring a specific runner

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Mockito provides several ways to initialise mocks automatically. The oldest approach is MockitoJUnitRunner, a JUnit 4 runner you put on your test class with @RunWith(MockitoJUnitRunner.class). It processes @Mock, @Spy, and @InjectMocks annotations before each test. The problem is it is tightly coupled to JUnit 4 and cannot be used with JUnit 5.

MockitoExtension is the JUnit 5 equivalent — you annotate with @ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class) and get the same automatic initialisation plus strict stubbing by default.

MockitoSession is a programmatic API that does the same initialisation work without being tied to any particular test framework. You call Mockito.mockitoSession().initMocks(this).startMocking() in a setup method and session.finishMocking() in a teardown method. It is useful in TestNG tests, custom frameworks, or when you want fine-grained control. It also enforces strict stubbing, catching unused stubs and unnecessary stubbings, which keeps tests clean.

For most Spring Boot projects using JUnit 5, MockitoExtension via @ExtendWith is the standard choice. MockitoSession is worth knowing about if you work in a mixed-framework environment or need to initialise mocks dynamically at runtime.

sections.title: Key Points
content: MockitoSession: programmatic, framework-agnostic, useful for TestNG or custom setups.
All three enforce strict stubbing to catch unused or wrong stubbings.

questions.question: How do you reset or clear a mock between tests, and when is that necessary?
questions.title: Resetting Mocks Between Tests
questions.direct_answer: Use Mockito.reset(mock) to wipe all stubbings and recorded interactions, but it is usually a design smell — prefer creating fresh mocks per test via @Mock with a proper test lifecycle.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of mock lifecycle and test isolation
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Sharing a single mock instance across all tests in a static field and then resetting it
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that Mockito.reset() is a code smell indicating shared state; the fix is per-test mock creation

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Mockito.reset(mock) clears all stubbings and recorded interactions on a mock, returning it to a pristine state. Technically it works, but in practice calling reset() is almost always a sign of a design problem in your test setup.

The problem it tries to solve is usually caused by sharing a single mock instance across multiple tests — for example, putting a mock in a static field or in a @BeforeAll setup. When tests share mocks, stubbings from test A can leak into test B, causing intermittent failures.

The correct fix is to let Mockito create a fresh mock before each test, which is exactly what @Mock with @ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class) or @BeforeEach setup does. Each @Mock-annotated field gets a brand new mock instance before every test method, so there is nothing to reset.

There is one legitimate use case: when you are using a Spring application context that is shared across tests for performance reasons (with @SpringBootTest and context caching), and you inject a @MockBean that lives in the application context. After a test that stubs that bean, the stub persists for the next test. In that scenario, calling Mockito.reset() in a @BeforeEach or @AfterEach is reasonable and common practice in Spring integration test suites.

sections.title: Key Points
content: Mockito.reset(mock) clears all stubbings and interactions on the mock.
Needing reset() usually indicates shared mock state — a test design smell.
Fix: use @Mock with @ExtendWith so each test gets a fresh mock automatically.
Legitimate use: shared @MockBean in Spring context tests where resetting per test is intentional.
